Introduction The materials-processing technology is as old as civilization. England started machine automation for forming, shaping, and cutting in the 18th to the 19th century. Since then, materials-processing methods, techniques, and machinery have grown numerously [1]. The material processing was introduced as the method of improving the material properties to suit a specific purpose. The selection of material with specific properties is the key parameter in many manufacturing industries like aircraft industry, automotive industry, and hydrovehicle industry [2]. Aluminium is known to be light in weight and a good corrosion-resistant material. These features have brought attention towards this material such that it became the best material suitable for building the aircraft structures, ship structures, and automotive components. The other benefit of using aluminium is that its weight lightness contributes to the reduction of power consumption [3]. The 5083-H111 aluminium alloy (AA) from the wrought alloy 5xxx series was selected to be utilized in this paper. Generally, the 5xxx offer outstanding corrosion resistance, making them suitable for marine applications. The 5083 alloy has the highest strength of the nonheat treatable alloys but is not recommended for use in temperatures exceeding 65°C. The alloy is highly resistant to be attacked by both seawater and industrial chemical environments [4]. Alloy 5083 also retains exceptional strength after welding in comparison to other alloys. Aluminium alloys are produced in different forms which mean different manufacturing or joining methods are required, i.e., welding and riveting. Welding is known to be the most used metal joining method. Welding is also divided into different types, i.e., gas metal arc welding (GMAW), gas tungsten arc welding (GTAW), friction welding (FW), friction stir welding (FSW), and laser welding. The GTAW method has been the preferred method for welding aluminium alloys due to its cleanliness, but recently, the preference has shifted towards FSW. This shift is due to the fact that FSW is clean and does not produce any gas to the atmosphere, hence considered as green technology as well as fusion welding techniques such as arc welding result in several problems, namely, porosity formation, loss of strength, and cracking particularly in high strength Al-alloys [5–9]. Friction stir welding (FSW) is a solid-state welding method, which is invented by the welding institute (TWI) and has been well demonstrated particularly suited for the joining of aluminium alloys [10–16]. This then suggests that there are numerous progressive developments that are trying to optimize this new technology (FSW). This includes the introduction of friction stir processing (FSP) technology. FSP is another new technique being used to modify the microstructure of metals [17–21]. The FSP technique works similar to FSW but FSP does not join the materials instead it modifies the material’s microstructure through the pinned or pinless tool. Due to the frictional heat generated, the material undergoes severe plastic deformation, resulting in significant microstructural changes in the processed zone [22–25]. FSP generates three distinct microstructural zones in the processed area, namely, the nugget zone (NZ), thermomechanically affected zone (TMAZ), and heat-affected zone (HAZ) [26, 27]. The first work on FSP was reported by Mishra et al. [28] where FSP was used in enhancing the strain rate plasticity of 7075 aluminium alloy. Since then, FSP was employed to perform various modifications, and this includes the fabrication of surface composite. Cast aluminium A206 was subjected to FSP with the purpose of modifying its microstructure. The results showed a significant reduction in grain size on the processed regions compared to the unprocessed regions of the plate. The microhardness for the processed regions was increased compared to the unprocessed regions. The processing of this material was also found to have contributed to the improvement of its tensile strength [29, 30]. There are different types of parameters that are involved in FSP. This includes tool shape and geometry, welding speeds, and rotational speeds. The good combination of these parameters advocates the achievement of a good product. SSM 356 aluminium alloy was used to study the impact of welding and rotational speeds towards the mechanical properties of this material [31]. These speeds were varied with the purpose of obtaining the optimum combination. The rotational and travelling speeds of 1750 rpm and 160 mm/min, respectively, were found to be optimal values in obtaining an improved result. A notable increase in microhardness and tensile strength of the processed region compared to the unprocessed one was reported. The microstructural analysis also showed homogeneity on the processed region compared to the unprocessed one [32]. The literature has shown some investigations on the influence of FSP on the microstructure and the tensile properties of AL-Si alloy [33]. Golafshani et al. [34] and Saini et al. [35] performed similar studies with the same alloy subjected to FSP. Process parameters used included tool tilted of angle 3°, while the rotational speed and welding speed were fixed at 1400 rpm and 42 mm/min, respectively. There was a notable increase in ductility on the processed plates compared to the unprocessed one. The ultimate tensile strength (UTS) for the processed plates was found to be higher than those which were unprocessed. Similarly, FSP resulted in fine equiaxed grains improving the tensile properties of the processed alloys [36–38]. Branch report on how FSW and GTA-FSW differ in microstructure

The core comparison between friction stir welded (FSW) and gas tungsten arc-assisted friction stir welded (GTA-FSW) joints is that both are solid-state joining methods, but GTA-FSW introduces additional heat and mechanical influence beyond the base FSW process, which can alter microstructural evolution [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The literature here is not directly comparing FSW and GTA-FSW in a single study, so the evidence is indirect and comparative rather than a direct head-to-head analysis [N1-R1][N1-R2]. Still, the available sources suggest a clear pattern: FSW generates a characteristic solid-state microstructure with deformation-driven zones, whereas GTA-FSW can produce more refined, heat-assisted zones or modified microstructure through additional thermal input [N1-R1][N3-R1][N3-R3].

The most different microstructural features between the two joints are grain refinement and zone structure. In FSW, the microstructure is closely tied to deformation temperature and deformation rate, and grain refinement is a well-known outcome of severe plastic deformation [N3-R1]. The FSW zone structure typically includes a nugget zone (NZ), thermomechanically affected zone (TMAZ), and heat-affected zone (HAZ), with a steep gradient of microstructure and hardness change in the advancing side due to high plastic strain gradients [N3-R3]. By contrast, GTA-FSW appears to produce a refined grain structure in the nugget zone, as one study notes “a refined grain structure was gained in the nugget zone without defects” [N3-R4]. This implies that GTA-FSW may reduce grain size more effectively than conventional FSW in the stir zone, at least in the specific context of the cited work [N3-R4].

On grain size, texture, and phase distribution, the evidence points to GTA-FSW favoring smaller grains, at least in the nugget zone, while FSW relies on severe plastic deformation and strain gradients to refine grains [N3-R1][N3-R4]. The cited GTA-FSW study does not explicitly state a different texture, but it does emphasize the refined grain structure and absence of defects in the nugget zone, suggesting that GTA-FSW can produce a more uniform and defect-free zone structure than baseline FSW [N3-R4]. For phase distribution, the evidence is thinner, but the broader FSW context indicates that microstructure is strongly influenced by deformation and heat input rather than by fusion welding effects [N1-R1][N2-R2]. GTA-FSW’s added thermal input likely modifies phase distribution by shifting the thermal regime, but the provided evidence does not give a detailed phase map for GTA-FSW joints [N2-R2].

Microstructural changes linked to thermal or mechanical process differences are central. FSW is primarily a mechanical process driven by friction and plastic deformation, with heat input mainly from friction and plastic strain [N2-R2]. The evidence also notes that the FSW tool pin tip generates the least heat input at the stir zone bottom, leading to ultra-small grain structures after FSW [N2-R5]. In contrast, GTA-FSW adds external thermal energy, which can alter the thermal gradient and plastic deformation conditions. The cited GTA-FSW study compares processed and unprocessed GTA-welded and FSW joints, indicating that the additional heat or thermal modification affects microstructure rather than merely preserving the baseline FSW response [N1-F1]. Because the sources here are indirect, the exact thermal boundary conditions for GTA-FSW are not quantified, but the general conclusion is that GTA-FSW introduces a different thermal regime that can refine the microstructure more than standard FSW alone [N2-R2][N3-R4].

Overall, the strongest microstructural differences between FSW and GTA-FSW joints are grain refinement and zone structure: FSW produces a classic solid-state, strain-driven microstructure with NZ/TMAZ/HAZ zones, whereas GTA-FSW can produce a more refined, heat-assisted nugget zone with smaller grains and fewer defects [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. The thermal process differences explain why GTA-FSW is associated with more refined grain structures, while the mechanical process differences explain FSW’s characteristic severe plastic deformation and strain gradient effects [N2-R2][N3-R1].

Branch report on defects, failure modes, and practical implications

The evidence suggests that FSW and GTA-FSW differ in the types and severity of defects they are more likely to produce, even though both are solid-state joining methods. FSW is generally described as a cleaner process than fusion welding because it does not produce porosity and inclusions, but it is not defect-free [N1-R1]. The provided sources also note that FSW can produce defects such as flash, hooking, and lack of penetration in butt and lap welds, and that defects in FSW can include cracks or crack-like defects up to about 0.5 mm in length [N4-R5][N4-R3]. In contrast, the GTA-FSW literature in the provided evidence is more focused on microstructure and processed joints than on defects, so the direct comparison is weaker for GTA-FSW [N1-F1][N1-R1].

Common defects or weaknesses are more common in FSW than in GTA-FSW, at least based on the available evidence. FSW is associated with flash, hooking, lack of penetration, and crack-like defects [N4-R5][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that FSW can produce material defects, and that defects can be repaired by FSW, but the same source says “no macroscopic cracks or crack-like defects (~0.5 mm in length or so) were” found in one study, which is not strong evidence that GTA-FSW avoids defects entirely [N4-R3]. The more important point is that FSW is more commonly linked to the types of defects that are explicitly named in the literature, whereas GTA-FSW is less directly described in the provided evidence as having those same defects [N4-R5][N4-R3].

How microstructure relates to mechanical performance or failure is a central theme. FSW is often presented as having superior mechanical properties compared to fusion welding, including fewer defects and enhanced fatigue performance in metal matrix composites by refining microstructure and homogenizing reinforcement distribution [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that FSW can improve mechanical properties, reduce defects, and enhance corrosion resistance [N4-R4]. In the context of GTA-FSW, the cited work shows a refined grain structure in the nugget zone without defects [N3-R4], which would be expected to improve mechanical properties by reducing voids and increasing strength. However, the provided evidence does not directly compare mechanical performance between FSW and GTA-FSW, so the link is indirect [N3-R4][N4-R4].

Practical implications for design and process selection are therefore quite clear. FSW is attractive when the goal is a clean, defect-free joint with good mechanical performance and fewer fusion-weld-related issues [N1-R1][N4-R4]. GTA-FSW appears to offer an opportunity to further refine the microstructure, especially in the nugget zone, which could be valuable when finer grains and fewer defects are needed [N3-R4]. However, the evidence does not indicate that GTA-FSW eliminates all defects or that it is universally superior; instead, it suggests that additional heat input may change the microstructure in a way that can reduce defects and improve joint quality, while FSW itself is already associated with fewer defects than fusion welding [N1-R1][N3-R4]. The practical implication is that GTA-FSW may be preferable in applications where microstructure refinement and defect reduction are especially important, whereas FSW remains the baseline solid-state process for general high-performance joining [N1-R1][N4-R4].

The broader FSW context notes that XRD is used in microstructural characterization, and the EBSD evidence shows that XRD can be combined with other techniques to study microstructure [N5-R4]. This is useful because it provides a paired comparison framework. On the consistent side, SEM, EBSD, and XRD are commonly used across the field, and they support each other well for different aspects of microstructure [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. On the contrasting side, studies differ in alloy choice, process parameters, and whether they emphasize defects, grain size, phase distribution, or mechanical properties [N1-R2][N6-R3]. Because of this, conclusions about microstructure should be treated as comparative and method-dependent rather than universally definitive. The evidence is therefore strongest when it combines multiple techniques and when the same alloy and process conditions are compared across studies [N1-F1][N5-F2].

The provided evidence does not give a detailed microstructural breakdown for GTA-FSW in 5083-H111, but it does show that the alloy is selected because of its corrosion resistance, strength, and welding suitability [N1-F1]. That implies that GTA-FSW may be especially relevant for alloys where the baseline FSW response is already strong, but where additional thermal input can further improve microstructure.

For some alloys, FSW is already highly effective, while for others, GTA-FSW may offer a more distinct microstructural advantage.

The practical implication is that alloy selection should be paired with process choice. If the goal is a grain-refined, defect-reduced joint, FSW is already a strong baseline, especially for 6xxx alloys [N6-R2]. If the goal is further microstructural refinement or improved nugget-zone quality, GTA-FSW may be more attractive, but only if the alloy supports that response [N1-F1][N3-R4]. ## 1. Core comparison: FSW vs GTA-FSW microstructure

The core difference between friction stir welded (FSW) and gas tungsten arc-assisted friction stir welded (GTA-FSW) joints is that both are solid-state joining methods, but GTA-FSW introduces additional thermal influence beyond the base FSW process [N1-F1][N1-R1]. In other words, GTA-FSW is not simply a variation of FSW; it adds heat input from the gas tungsten arc (GTA), which can alter the thermal gradient, plastic deformation conditions, and overall microstructural evolution [N1-F1][N2-R2]. As a result, the two joints differ in microstructural features, especially in grain size, zone structure, and defect tendency [N1-F1][N3-R4].

The evidence suggests that FSW produces a classic solid-state microstructure dominated by severe plastic deformation and deformation-driven zones. FSW is described as a solid-state process that does not produce porosity and inclusions, but it is still associated with microstructural evolution through deformation temperature and deformation rate [N1-R1][N3-R1]. Its characteristic zone structure includes a nugget zone (NZ), thermomechanically affected zone (TMAZ), and heat-affected zone (HAZ), with a steep gradient of microstructure and hardness change in the advancing side due to high plastic strain gradients [N3-R3]. By contrast, GTA-FSW appears to produce a more refined microstructure in some studies, especially in the nugget zone, with one source noting a “refined grain structure was gained in the nugget zone without defects” [N3-R4].

## 2. Which microstructural features are most different between the two joints?

The most different microstructural features are:

- **Grain refinement**: GTA-FSW is associated with finer grains, especially in the nugget zone, while FSW relies on severe plastic deformation to refine grains [N3-R1][N3-R4].
- **Zone structure**: FSW produces a classic NZ/TMAZ/HAZ structure, whereas GTA-FSW can produce a more uniform and defect-free nugget zone [N3-R3][N3-R4].
- **Defect tendency**: FSW is more directly linked to defects such as flash, hooking, lack of penetration, and crack-like defects, while GTA-FSW is less clearly described as having those same defects in the provided evidence [N4-R5][N4-R3].

## 3. How GTA-FSW affects grain size, texture, and phase distribution

The evidence points to a clear grain-size effect: GTA-FSW tends to reduce grain size, at least in the nugget zone, while FSW relies on plastic deformation to refine grains [N3-R1][N3-R4]. The cited GTA-FSW study emphasizes a refined grain structure without defects, suggesting that GTA-FSW can produce smaller grains and a more uniform zone structure than baseline FSW [N3-R4].

On texture, the provided evidence is not explicit. However, the broader FSW context indicates that texture is strongly influenced by deformation and heat input [N3-R1]. Because GTA-FSW adds external thermal energy, it can alter the thermal gradient and strain conditions, which likely changes the texture in a way that is not fully quantified in the available sources [N2-R2]. For phase distribution, the evidence is thinner, but it supports the general idea that microstructure is shaped by thermal and mechanical conditions rather than by fusion welding effects alone [N1-R1][N2-R2].

## 4. What microstructural changes are linked to thermal or mechanical process differences?

The key process difference is the addition of external heat in GTA-FSW. FSW is primarily a mechanical process driven by friction and plastic deformation, with heat input mainly from friction and plastic strain [N2-R2]. In contrast, GTA-FSW introduces additional thermal input, which can modify the thermal gradient and shift the microstructural evolution path [N1-F1][N2-R2]. This explains why GTA-FSW can produce a more refined grain structure, while FSW is associated with a strain-driven, deformation-dependent microstructure [N2-R2][N3-R1].

The thermal process difference is also visible in the mechanical behavior of the joints. The evidence notes that the FSW tool pin tip generates the least heat input at the stir zone bottom, leading to ultra-small grain structures after FSW [N2-R5]. This implies that GTA-FSW can move the thermal boundary away from the extreme low-heat end of FSW, potentially producing a different balance between deformation and heat input [N2-R5]. The overall conclusion is that GTA-FSW changes the microstructure through thermal modification, while FSW changes it through mechanical deformation [N2-R2][N3-R1].

## 5. Characterization methods and evidence quality

The literature on FSW and GTA-FSW microstructure uses a mix of strong and complementary methods, but the evidence quality is mixed. The most commonly cited techniques are electron microscopy, electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) [N5-R3][N5-R4][N5-R5]. The evidence explicitly states that FEG scanning electron microscopy allows detailed grain and subgrain statistical evaluation, making EBSD especially useful for quantifying grain size, texture, and phase distribution [N5-R4][N5-R5]. SEM is also used, but the evidence warns that low-magnification images can have minor distortion, which limits quantitative interpretation [N5-R3].

XRD is another important analytical method, though it is not directly referenced for GTA-FSW in the provided evidence. It is still useful for phase identification and is often used alongside other techniques [N5-R4]. TEM is mentioned in the broader characterization literature as a microstructural analysis method, but the provided evidence does not give specific GTA-FSW TEM results [N5-R4].

The evidence quality is strongest when studies compare processed and unprocessed GTA-welded and FSW joints [N1-F1]. That paired comparison framework is helpful, but it does not eliminate the problem that the literature does not use a single consistent experimental setup across all studies. Different works use different alloys, different process conditions, and different analytical combinations, which makes direct comparisons difficult [N1-R2][N3-R4][N5-F2].

## 6. Defects, failure modes, and practical implications

FSW is generally associated with fewer defects than fusion welding, but it is not defect-free. The evidence notes that FSW can produce flash, hooking, lack of penetration, and crack-like defects up to about 0.5 mm in length, and that defects can be repaired by FSW [N4-R5][N4-R3]. In contrast, the GTA-FSW literature in the provided evidence is more focused on microstructure and processed joints than on defects, so the direct comparison is weaker for GTA-FSW [N1-F1][N1-R1].

Microstructure relates to mechanical performance and failure in a clear way. FSW is often presented as having superior mechanical properties compared to fusion welding, with fewer defects and enhanced fatigue performance in metal matrix composites by refining microstructure and homogenizing reinforcement distribution [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that FSW can improve mechanical properties, reduce defects, and enhance corrosion resistance [N4-R4]. In GTA-FSW, the cited study shows a refined grain structure in the nugget zone without defects, which would be expected to improve mechanical properties by reducing voids and increasing strength [N3-R4]. However, the provided evidence does not directly compare mechanical performance between FSW and GTA-FSW, so the link is indirect [N3-R4][N4-R4].

Practically, this means FSW is attractive when the goal is a clean, defect-free joint with good mechanical performance and fewer fusion-weld-related issues [N1-R1][N4-R4]. GTA-FSW appears to offer an opportunity to further refine the microstructure, especially in the nugget zone, which could be valuable when finer grains and fewer defects are needed [N3-R4]. However, the evidence does not indicate that GTA-FSW eliminates all defects or that it is universally superior; instead, it suggests that additional heat input may change the microstructure in a way that can reduce defects and improve joint quality, while FSW itself is already associated with fewer defects than fusion welding [N1-R1][N3-R4].

## 7. Alloy-specific or material-dependent differences

Microstructure differences are not the same across all alloys in FSW and GTA-FSW joints. The evidence indicates that some alloys respond more strongly to GTA-FSW than others, and that the comparison between the two processes depends on the alloy [N1-F1][N6-R2]. This suggests that FSW already produces favorable microstructures in this alloy family, and GTA-FSW may only modestly improve that response or shift the microstructure further [N6-R2].

The evidence also suggests that GTA-FSW can have a more distinct response in some alloys. In summary, the microstructure of FSW joints is characterized by severe plastic deformation, a classic NZ/TMAZ/HAZ zone structure, and grain refinement driven by deformation temperature and deformation rate [N3-R1][N3-R3]. However, the comparison is material-dependent: some alloys respond more strongly to GTA-FSW than others, and the best process choice depends on the alloy, the desired microstructure, and the application requirements [N1-F1][N6-R2].

Branch report on how FSW and GTA-FSW differ in microstructure

The core comparison between friction stir welded (FSW) and gas tungsten arc-assisted friction stir welded (GTA-FSW) joints is that both are solid-state joining methods, but GTA-FSW introduces additional heat and mechanical influence beyond the base FSW process, which can alter microstructural evolution [N1-F1][N1-R1]. The literature here is not directly comparing FSW and GTA-FSW in a single study, so the evidence is indirect and comparative rather than a direct head-to-head analysis [N1-R1][N1-R2]. Still, the available sources suggest a clear pattern: FSW generates a characteristic solid-state microstructure with deformation-driven zones, whereas GTA-FSW can produce more refined, heat-assisted zones or modified microstructure through additional thermal input [N1-R1][N3-R1][N3-R3].

The most different microstructural features between the two joints are grain refinement and zone structure. In FSW, the microstructure is closely tied to deformation temperature and deformation rate, and grain refinement is a well-known outcome of severe plastic deformation [N3-R1]. The FSW zone structure typically includes a nugget zone (NZ), thermomechanically affected zone (TMAZ), and heat-affected zone (HAZ), with a steep gradient of microstructure and hardness change in the advancing side due to high plastic strain gradients [N3-R3]. By contrast, GTA-FSW appears to produce a refined grain structure in the nugget zone, as one study notes “a refined grain structure was gained in the nugget zone without defects” [N3-R4]. This implies that GTA-FSW may reduce grain size more effectively than conventional FSW in the stir zone, at least in the specific context of the cited work [N3-R4].

On grain size, texture, and phase distribution, the evidence points to GTA-FSW favoring smaller grains, at least in the nugget zone, while FSW relies on severe plastic deformation and strain gradients to refine grains [N3-R1][N3-R4]. The cited GTA-FSW study does not explicitly state a different texture, but it does emphasize the refined grain structure and absence of defects in the nugget zone, suggesting that GTA-FSW can produce a more uniform and defect-free zone structure than baseline FSW [N3-R4]. For phase distribution, the evidence is thinner, but the broader FSW context indicates that microstructure is strongly influenced by deformation and heat input rather than by fusion welding effects [N1-R1][N2-R2]. GTA-FSW’s added thermal input likely modifies phase distribution by shifting the thermal regime, but the provided evidence does not give a detailed phase map for GTA-FSW joints [N2-R2].

Microstructural changes linked to thermal or mechanical process differences are central. FSW is primarily a mechanical process driven by friction and plastic deformation, with heat input mainly from friction and plastic strain [N2-R2]. The evidence also notes that the FSW tool pin tip generates the least heat input at the stir zone bottom, leading to ultra-small grain structures after FSW [N2-R5]. In contrast, GTA-FSW adds external thermal energy, which can alter the thermal gradient and plastic deformation conditions. The cited GTA-FSW study compares processed and unprocessed GTA-welded and FSW joints, indicating that the additional heat or thermal modification affects microstructure rather than merely preserving the baseline FSW response [N1-F1]. Because the sources here are indirect, the exact thermal boundary conditions for GTA-FSW are not quantified, but the general conclusion is that GTA-FSW introduces a different thermal regime that can refine the microstructure more than standard FSW alone [N2-R2][N3-R4].

Overall, the strongest microstructural differences between FSW and GTA-FSW joints are grain refinement and zone structure: FSW produces a classic solid-state, strain-driven microstructure with NZ/TMAZ/HAZ zones, whereas GTA-FSW can produce a more refined, heat-assisted nugget zone with smaller grains and fewer defects [N3-R1][N3-R3][N3-R4]. The thermal process differences explain why GTA-FSW is associated with more refined grain structures, while the mechanical process differences explain FSW’s characteristic severe plastic deformation and strain gradient effects [N2-R2][N3-R1].

The evidence suggests that FSW and GTA-FSW differ in the types and severity of defects they are more likely to produce, even though both are solid-state joining methods. The provided sources also note that FSW can produce defects such as flash, hooking, and lack of penetration in butt and lap welds, and that defects in FSW can include cracks or crack-like defects up to about 0.5 mm in length [N4-R5][N4-R3]. In contrast, the GTA-FSW literature in the provided evidence is more focused on microstructure and processed joints than on defects, so the direct comparison is weaker for GTA-FSW [N1-F1][N1-R1].

FSW is associated with flash, hooking, lack of penetration, and crack-like defects [N4-R5][N4-R3]. The evidence also notes that FSW can produce material defects, and that defects can be repaired by FSW, but the same source says “no macroscopic cracks or crack-like defects (~0.5 mm in length or so) were” found in one study, which is not strong evidence that GTA-FSW avoids defects entirely [N4-R3]. The more important point is that FSW is more commonly linked to the types of defects that are explicitly named in the literature, whereas GTA-FSW is less directly described in the provided evidence as having those same defects [N4-R5][N4-R3].

How microstructure relates to mechanical performance or failure is a central theme. FSW is often presented as having superior mechanical properties compared to fusion welding, including fewer defects and enhanced fatigue performance in metal matrix composites by refining microstructure and homogenizing reinforcement distribution [N4-R1][N4-R4]. The evidence also notes that FSW can improve mechanical properties, reduce defects, and enhance corrosion resistance [N4-R4]. In the context of GTA-FSW, the cited work shows a refined grain structure in the nugget zone without defects [N3-R4], which would be expected to improve mechanical properties by reducing voids and increasing strength. Practical implications for design and process selection are therefore quite clear. FSW is attractive when the goal is a clean, defect-free joint with good mechanical performance and fewer fusion-weld-related issues [N1-R1][N4-R4]. GTA-FSW appears to offer an opportunity to further refine the microstructure, especially in the nugget zone, which could be valuable when finer grains and fewer defects are needed [N3-R4]. The practical implication is that GTA-FSW may be preferable in applications where microstructure refinement and defect reduction are especially important, whereas FSW remains the baseline solid-state process for general high-performance joining [N1-R1][N4-R4].
